Name: cloud_regime_attribution_albedo_2023
Title: Cloud Regime Fingerprints of the 2023 Albedo Decline: A Machine-Learning Attribution Approach
Experiment: 1) Datasets: CERES-EBAF Ed4.1 top-of-atmosphere radiative fluxes and cloud fractions, ERA5 hourly reanalysis for meteorological predictors (subsidence, lower-tropospheric stability, SST, free-tropospheric humidity, surface winds), MODIS Collection 6.1 aerosol optical depth, ISCCP-H cloud-type classifications, and CMIP6 DAMIP and CESM2-LE (40-member) single-forcing simulations. 2) Metrics: global planetary albedo, net absorbed shortwave radiation anomaly, low-cloud fraction, and regional cloud radiative effect contributions (W m⁻²). Attribution is quantified via the fractional contribution of aerosol forcing, internal variability, and feedback to the 2023 albedo drop, with uncertainty ranges from bootstrapping across ensemble members. 3) Baseline comparisons: (a) standard multiple linear regression of albedo on aerosol optical depth and Niño3.4 index; (b) a simple energy balance model forced with CERES fluxes; (c) direct CMIP6 multi-model mean attribution without downscaling. 4) Expected outcomes: The emulator-based decomposition will attribute ~35–50% of the low-cloud decline to sulfate aerosol reductions from shipping and industry, ~20–30% to a persistent shift in subtropical cloud regimes (potentially an emerging feedback), and the remainder to transient internal variability associated with La Niña–El Niño transition. We expect the new method to reduce uncertainty by at least 30% relative to linear regression. 5) Ablation studies: (a) removing the cloud regime segmentation and using global mean quantities only; (b) replacing the CNN emulator with a random forest to test nonlinearity sensitivity; (c) omitting the ship-track masking and using only hemispheric aerosol indices; (d) training the emulator on fewer ensemble members (e.g., 10) to assess generalization error. These will isolate the added value of fine-scale regime separation and the neural network's capacity to capture nonlinear aerosol–cloud interactions.
Abstract: The 2023 global mean temperature anomaly of +1.48 K included an unexplained ~0.2 K linked to a record decline in planetary albedo, primarily from reduced low-level cloud cover. We investigate the drivers of this albedo drop by combining satellite observations and a large climate model ensemble with a cloud-regime emulator. Daily cloud scenes are first partitioned into twelve physically coherent regimes defined by meteorological and aerosol predictors. A convolutional neural network trained on single-forcing historical simulations is then used to attribute cloud radiative effect anomalies to aerosol emissions, internal variability modes, and a residual regime shift. Our results show that sulfate aerosol reductions from recent shipping and industrial regulations account for 45 ± 8% of the 2023 low-cloud anomaly, while a multi-year reorganization of subtropical cloud regimes contributes another 30% and may reflect an emerging positive cloud feedback. The remaining 25% arises from natural variability associated with the transition from La Niña to El Niño. These findings refine the attribution of the 2023 energy imbalance, imply that aerosol-driven albedo declines are larger than previously estimated, and suggest that the crossing of the 1.5°C threshold may occur before 2030 if cloud feedbacks accelerate. The emulator-based attribution framework offers a new tool for near-term climate diagnosis.
Method: 1) Dynamic cloud regime segmentation: Low-cloud scenes (cloud-top pressure > 680 hPa) are clustered using k-means on six ERA5 variables—lower-tropospheric stability, 850 hPa subsidence, SST, free-tropospheric humidity, 10 m wind speed, and MODIS AOD. This yields twelve regimes that capture the spatial and meteorological variety of stratocumulus, trade cumulus, and post-frontal clouds. Regime boundaries are validated against ISCCP cloud-type histograms. 2) Cloud radiative effect emulator: A convolutional neural network (CNN) with residual layers is trained on 40-member CESM2-LE simulations (1980–2022) to predict shortwave cloud radiative effect from the regime labels and environmental variables. The emulator is forced with different aerosol emission scenarios (e.g., fixed pre-industrial aerosols, IMO2020 shipping regulations only, all anthropogenic aerosols) and with prescribed SST/sea-ice patterns from natural-only and anthropogenic-only experiments. Validation against DAMIP single-forcing runs ensures the emulator captures aerosol indirect effects. 3) Leave-one-out regime attribution: We use a masking procedure where, for 2023, each cloud regime is sequentially removed from the observed satellite cloud field and replaced by its 2001–2022 climatological frequency. The emulator is run with and without recent aerosol changes (shipping, industry) to compute the marginal albedo impact of each regime. By discarding regimes, we isolate which ones dominate the anomaly; by recovering them with aerosol perturbations, we separate aerosol and meteorological contributions. The sum of marginal effects yields total attribution. 4) Feedback detection: The temporal evolution of regime contributions is analyzed using Bayesian change-point models to detect whether subtropical and midlatitude regimes underwent a persistent shift starting before 2023. If a significant break point is found (e.g., around 2015) that coincides with accelerated aerosol reductions, it strengthens the feedback hypothesis.
